strengths: Addresses a practical problem with clear motivation: enhancing frozen CLIP models without costly re-embedding, relevant to deployed systems
Identifies and thoroughly demonstrates the score inflation problem when using similarity-based rewards, with both empirical evidence (Figure 5) and theoretical analysis (Appendix A.1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 datasets, 3 model scales, and 3 types of distribution shifts (multilingual, length, modality) with consistent improvements
Provides formal theoretical justification: proof that ranking-based reward is affine-invariant, ensuring robustness regardless of score scaling
Honest discussion of limitations with empirical support (e.g., Figure 7 showing language-dependent performance), not overstating applicability
Good qualitative analysis with concrete case studies demonstrating how GRAPE handles different distribution shifts effectively
Data efficiency analysis (Figure 4) shows the method achieves 94% of full performance with only 10% training data on some benchmarks
Plug-and-play design requiring no modifications to frozen retrievers or corpus embeddings increases practical deployment viability
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is applying existing GRPO with a simple ranking formula (Eq. 4); using ranking instead of similarity for ranking tasks is intuitive rather than innovative

Score inflation analysis only demonstrated on one dataset (Flickr30k-CN); lacks quantitative characterization across other tasks and no comparison with alternative solutions (e.g., other ranking losses)
Improvements are modest (~4.9% R@10 average) and lack statistical rigor: no significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; CIRR shows only 3.5% gains for larger models

Incomplete experimental comparisons: missing baselines with training-free methods (e.g., PlugIR mentioned but not compared), no ablation on ranking losses without policy gradient framework, different LLMs across tasks conflates variables

Reproducibility concerns: extremely small learning rate (5×10^-7) unjustified, only 1.5-2.5k training steps without convergence analysis, task-specific prompts suggest prompt engineering sensitivity, no ablations on K (number of rewrites) or format reward weight

Critical latency issue unaddressed: every query requires LLM rewriting before retrieval yet no runtime measurements provided; acknowledged as 'modest' without quantification, potentially prohibitive for interactive systems

Method effectiveness fundamentally bounded by LLM knowledge: Figure 7 shows severe performance degradation for low-resource languages, yet this critical limitation receives minimal analysis despite being acknowledged
Section 4.3 relies on qualitative examples rather than quantitative metrics; lacks systematic measurement of claimed mechanisms (token entropy, semantic enrichment quantification)
No statistical testing, error bars, or variance analysis; single learning curves provided without multiple random seeds

Missing critical ablations: no independent evaluation of format vs. ranking rewards, sensitivity to hyperparameters (learning rate, training steps), or comparison with simpler ranking-based alternatives

strengths: Well-motivated identification and analysis of score inflation phenomenon in similarity-based supervision, with clear theoretical justification through feature decomposition and empirical validation (Figure 5)
Principled ranking-based reward design with proven affine invariance properties and stable normalization via within-group statistics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 diverse benchmarks covering multilingual, long-form, and multimodal scenarios with consistent improvements
Impressive data efficiency results (94% performance with 10% data on Flickr30k-CN) valuable for cold-start scenarios
Practical plug-and-play approach that avoids costly corpus re-embedding and retriever retraining
Thorough ablation studies and failure mode analysis demonstrating robustness (14%→3% failure rate reduction)
Clear presentation with informative visualizations effectively explaining the approach and problem
weaknesses: Theoretical analysis of score inflation assumes specific feature decomposition (z = μ + ž) that may not precisely hold in practice; lacks formal convergence guarantees or sample complexity analysis
Unfair baseline comparison: similarity-based reward (Eq. 5) lacks normalization; comparison with normalized similarity baseline would be more convincing

Lack of justification for specific design choices: why linear reward mapping (Eq. 4)? Limited sensitivity analysis for functional forms; Table 6 shows minimal performance differences across group sizes K=2-8

Moderate improvements (4.9% average Recall@10) that are significant but not transformative; language-specific results (Figure 7) show minimal gains for low-resource languages, severely limiting applicability
Inference overhead mentioned but not quantified; latency analysis deferred to appendix without actual timing measurements—critical for practical deployment
Limited scope: CLIP-specific method with unclear generalization to other retrievers; no experiments with dense retrieval or other architectures
Incremental novelty: adapts existing GRPO algorithm with straightforward ranking-based reward; query rewriting for retrieval previously explored (ComCLIP, PlugIR)
Missing key experimental comparisons: no comparison with training-based finetuning methods or parameter-efficient tuning (LoRA, adapters); Table 4 uses non-controlled LLM baselines
No statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals despite modest improvements
Reproducibility concerns: code link missing, training time/computational requirements not specified, randomness/seed management not discussed
